musical.title: Annie
musical.vocal_style: Classic Broadway show tunes with a 1930s Depression-era flavour. Annie requires a real belt soprano with genuine brightness. Miss Hannigan is a character belt mezzo who should sound like someone whose cheerfulness has long since curdled. The score is warm, tuneful, and wonderfully accessible.
musical.synopsis: New York City, 1933. Annie is an irrepressibly optimistic orphan who escapes the miserable care of Miss Hannigan for a weekend with billionaire Oliver Warbucks — and discovers that, with enough spirit, anything is possible. Features one of the most famous songs in all of musical theatre.

roles.name: Annie
roles.description: One of the most iconic child roles in all of musical theatre. Annie is indestructible optimism in the face of genuine hardship — she has had a terrible life and she is completely, unshakeably certain that it will get better. 'Tomorrow' is the most famous song about hope in the commercial musical theatre canon.

vocal.style_notes: Bright, clear belt soprano — 'Tomorrow' must feel genuinely confident, not wistful. The voice should sound like someone who has decided to believe. Must be bright, warm, and real — not the performed brightness of a competition singer.

dance.notes: Annie should be an energetic, natural mover. Not technically demanding but must feel completely free and joyful in her body.

acting.notes: The optimism must be completely real, not forced. Annie has chosen hope — it's not naivety or ignorance. She knows her situation is bad and she has decided it will get better anyway. That specificity is everything.

casting_insights.why: One of the great iconic child roles in musical theatre history. 'Tomorrow' is known worldwide. An Annie performance is a career-defining moment.
casting_insights.common_casting: Young belt sopranos with natural charisma and real emotional intelligence. 'Tomorrow' is widely performed — a fresh, genuine interpretation is critical.

what_directors_look_for: 'Tomorrow' — the belt must be genuine and the optimism must be completely real
Natural stage presence and movement confidence
The emotional intelligence to make the hope feel chosen, not assumed
tips: Tomorrow is widely known — show something specific and real in your interpretation
The belt should feel effortless — Annie doesn't perform, she just sings
Don't play Annie as cute — she's practical, resourceful, and genuinely brave
common_mistakes: Playing the cuteness rather than the character
A warbly or wavering belt — 'Tomorrow' requires a strong, clear tone
Making Annie too precious — she's a scrappy kid, not a china doll

key_songs.title: Tomorrow
key_songs.notes: The signature song of the show and one of the most famous in musical theatre history. Must feel completely genuine.

key_songs.title: Maybe
key_songs.notes: Annie's yearning for her birth parents. Vulnerability beneath the optimism.

key_songs.title: It's the Hard-Knock Life
key_songs.notes: The orphans' sardonic commentary on their situation. Annie leads with genuine spirit.

key_songs.title: I Don't Need Anything But You
key_songs.notes: Annie and Warbucks's warming relationship — completely touching.

roles.name: Miss Hannigan
roles.description: The gin-addled, orphan-loathing head of the Hudson Street Home for Girls. Miss Hannigan is one of the great comic villains of family musical theatre — she's completely horrible but the audience secretly understands her. 'Little Girls' is one of the most hilariously committed complaint songs ever written.

vocal.style_notes: Character belt mezzo with the quality of someone who once had talent and has been professionally disappointed ever since. 'Little Girls' should sound like genuine despair delivered with tremendous flair.

dance.notes: Physical comedy is central. Miss Hannigan's physicality tells the whole story — she moves like someone who has given up on elegance but not on theatrical effect.

acting.notes: The key to Hannigan is that she is genuine — she really does hate children and her situation really is awful. She's not a caricature villain but a specific person whose life has deeply disappointed her. The comedy comes from total commitment.

casting_insights.why: One of the most beloved character comedy roles in family musical theatre. Miss Hannigan is frequently the audience favourite.
casting_insights.common_casting: Character belt mezzos with genuine dark comedy and physical commitment. Both voice and acting must be excellent.

what_directors_look_for: 'Little Girls' — the genuine commitment to the horror of children is the whole audition
Physical character specificity — every choice Hannigan makes tells us exactly who she is
The belt mezzo voice with character texture
tips: 'Little Girls' is the definitive audition — commit to it completely
Show the genuine despair underneath the comedy — Hannigan is not performing, she really feels this way
The gin-soaked quality of the character must feel physically real, not just indicated
common_mistakes: Playing Hannigan as pantomime villain — she's a specific, genuinely suffering person
Missing the dark comedy — Hannigan's horror at children must also be genuinely funny

key_songs.title: Little Girls
key_songs.notes: The definitive Miss Hannigan piece. A hymn to the horror of children, delivered with absolute conviction.

key_songs.title: Easy Street
key_songs.notes: Hannigan with Rooster and Lily. The scheming number — darkly funny fantasy.

roles.name: Oliver Warbucks
roles.description: The billionaire who discovers he has a heart through his weekend with Annie. Warbucks is a classic character transformation role — cold, efficient, and powerful at the start; genuinely loving and changed by the end. 'Something Was Missing' is one of the most quietly moving songs in the show.

vocal.style_notes: Warm, authoritative baritone. Warbucks doesn't have the most technically demanding material but every song should feel genuine and earned.

dance.notes: Warbucks moves with authority and dignity. Limited dance requirements but physical presence is important.

acting.notes: The transformation must feel completely genuine — Warbucks doesn't just change, he discovers a capacity for love he didn't know he had. The relationship with Annie must build organically.

casting_insights.why: 'Something Was Missing' and 'I Don't Need Anything But You' are genuinely touching character moments. An important anchor role for the show.
casting_insights.common_casting: Warm, authoritative baritones with genuine acting ability and the stage presence to be convincingly the most powerful man in every room.

what_directors_look_for: Physical authority and genuine warmth that emerges across the show
The transformation must be believable — Warbucks must start genuinely cold
'Something Was Missing' — quiet, real, not sentimental
tips: Start the show as someone who has organised his life to not need love
Let Annie visibly unguard you — don't telegraph the transformation
common_mistakes: Starting the show as too warm — the transformation has nowhere to go if Warbucks is already soft

key_songs.title: Something Was Missing
key_songs.notes: Warbucks's quiet realisation of what he's been missing in his life.

key_songs.title: I Don't Need Anything But You
key_songs.notes: The genuinely touching celebration of the new family.

roles.name: Rooster Hannigan & Lily St. Regis
roles.description: Miss Hannigan's scheming brother and his dim, glamorous girlfriend. Rooster is slick, smooth, and completely amoral. Lily is wonderfully vapid. 'Easy Street' is a deliciously entertaining villainy number that gives both characters their best moments.

vocal.style_notes: Rooster: smooth character tenor or baritone. Lily: bright, breathy soprano with comedic quality. Both need 1930s musical comedy style.

dance.notes: Easy Street requires specific 1930s style choreography with genuine entertainment value.

acting.notes: Rooster and Lily should feel like a specific type of 1930s entertainment duo — slick, unreliable, and genuinely funny about their own awfulness.

casting_insights.why: 'Easy Street' is one of the show's great entertainment numbers. Both roles are genuinely fun to play.
casting_insights.common_casting: Rooster: smooth character performers with period style and dark comedy. Lily: a comic soprano with genuine physical comedy and the ability to play wonderfully dim.

what_directors_look_for: 'Easy Street' can be used as an audition trio with Hannigan
1930s musical comedy style — the characters live entirely in a specific aesthetic
Genuine comic chemistry between Rooster and Lily
tips: Find the specific 1930s quality — they're not modern comedy characters in period costume
common_mistakes: Missing the period style — the whole comedy depends on living in the 1930s aesthetic

key_songs.title: Easy Street
key_songs.notes: The scheming fantasy number with Hannigan. Perfectly judged comic villainy.

roles.name: Grace Farrell
roles.description: Warbucks's devoted secretary who selects Annie and becomes central to the family that forms. Grace is warm, efficient, and quietly romantic. She is the bridge between Warbucks's world and Annie's world.

vocal.style_notes: Warm, clear soprano mezzo. Grace's vocal quality should match her character — capable, warm, real.

dance.notes: Grace moves with professional efficiency and natural warmth.

acting.notes: Grace is the heart of the show's adult world — she feels what Warbucks hasn't yet let himself feel.

casting_insights.why: An important supporting role that holds the adult emotional world together.
casting_insights.common_casting: Warm sopranos with genuine stage presence and professional grace.

what_directors_look_for: The genuine love for Annie that develops — Grace sees her clearly from the start
tips: Show the warmth before the professional quality — Grace's feeling is her defining characteristic
common_mistakes: Playing Grace as entirely functional — she has real emotional investment in the story

key_songs.title: I Think I'm Gonna Like It Here
key_songs.notes: Grace introduces Annie to Warbucks's household. Warm, gentle, full of real feeling.

roles.name: Orphan Ensemble (Molly, Kate, Pepper, Duffy, July, Tessie)
roles.description: The six named orphans are the beating heart of the show — their ensemble scenes, particularly 'It's the Hard-Knock Life' and 'You're Never Fully Dressed Without a Smile', are among the show's most joyful moments. Each orphan has a distinct personality and needs to feel like a specific, real child.

vocal.style_notes: Natural children's voices. Genuine brightness and energy rather than performed sweetness.

dance.notes: The orphan choreography should feel energetic and slightly chaotic — these are unsupervised children. Hard-Knock Life requires committed physical performance.

acting.notes: Each orphan must feel like a real, specific child. The ensemble's spirit is what makes the orphanage scenes come alive.

casting_insights.why: Outstanding early stage experience in one of the most beloved family musicals ever written.
casting_insights.common_casting: Young performers with genuine energy and stage presence. Natural, individual character work over polished technique.

what_directors_look_for: Individual character distinctness — each orphan is a specific person, not a generic child
The ability to be genuinely funny in the ensemble scenes
tips: Know which orphan you're right for and show their specific personality
Hard-Knock Life should feel genuinely rebellious, not just cute
common_mistakes: Playing generic sweet child rather than a specific, distinct character

key_songs.title: It's the Hard-Knock Life
key_songs.notes: The show's great comic orphan number. Physical, energetic, genuinely funny.

key_songs.title: You're Never Fully Dressed Without a Smile
key_songs.notes: The radio broadcast number — pure joy.
